roles.summary: I make a real-time voice AI agent honest, safe and fast. Most of my work sits in the parts users never see: what the agent is allowed to read and do, how it behaves when data is missing, how quickly it speaks, and the native Mac app that listens to calls.

sections.title: An agent that says "I don't know" instead of inventing
sections.body: The agent treated "I couldn't read that" the same as "there's nothing there", then filled the gap with something plausible. I changed the contract rather than the prompt.
bullets: Every result now states what it covered and whether it was cut short.
Every data source declares what an empty answer actually means, so "unknown" can never be passed along as "empty".
The honesty rules live in a platform layer that no persona or prompt edit can remove.
sections.lesson: Lesson: most hallucinations I fixed weren't model problems. They were data contracts that let silence look like an answer.

sections.title: Default-deny permissions for an agent with real access
sections.body: An agent that can read a whole organisation's data and write to other systems needs hard limits, not polite instructions.
bullets: An authorization rail where broader reads must be explicitly offered and accepted, bound to the exact query.
Approvals that freeze what the human agreed to, so the action can't change afterwards.
Refusals that look identical to "not found", so they leak nothing.
Closed cross-tenant read and write paths, a file path-traversal bug and a database-permission bypass.
Made it impossible at compile time to write a raw error into the logs.

sections.title: Voice that answers while you're still listening
sections.body: I built the streaming pipeline, then measured every stage of a spoken turn and optimised against the measurements, not against how a demo felt.
bullets: The model's words are spoken sentence by sentence as they're generated.
Interruptions and background noise are handled without cutting people off.
Code and raw data are never read aloud.
sections.lesson: Lesson: the biggest wins came from changing the order of work, not from a faster model.

sections.title: A native Mac app that knows who's talking (Swift)
bullets: Replaced audio downsampling that had no filter (it folded noise into the speech band) with a streaming windowed-sinc resampler.
Fixed speech streams closing silently, which split three people on a call into ten "speakers", with keep-alives and buffering so a call's first seconds aren't lost.
On-device detection of who's speaking on screen (Vision OCR; no image ever leaves the Mac), combined with calendar data and introductions.
A speaker is named only when the evidence agrees; otherwise the line stays unnamed rather than guessed.

sections.title: Background work that recovers and runs exactly once
bullets: Scheduled routines that are time-zone safe, with durable leasing and recovery, exactly-once publication and default-deny permissions.
Preparation driven by events (calendar changes, CRM syncs, finished calls) instead of polling, so work is ready before the user asks.
Approval-gated write-back to CRMs: one approval, decided on desktop, chat or web.

sections.title: How I work
sections.body: I work AI-assisted, but I own every change: written plans first, multiple review rounds including independent reviewers, mutation testing to prove the tests can actually fail, and proofs against a real database rather than mocks. When a review proves my fix wrong, I revert it.

roles.summary: I run engineering end to end for a venture-backed startup: the AI assistant, the data platform behind it, cloud operations, and every release to the App Store. I also review, integrate and ship the rest of the team's work.

sections.title: From too slow to usable
sections.body: I inherited an AI assistant that took 72–122 seconds to show anything. I rebuilt it as a Python/FastAPI service with tool orchestration, retrieval and structured responses the mobile app can render. Then I profiled every stage: deadlines, concurrency, and deterministic fast paths where a model call wasn't needed. First results now arrive in under 10 seconds, and keyword search went from 10.6 s to 53 ms.
sections.lesson: Lesson: passing unit tests didn't mean the answers were useful, so I built golden and adversarial evaluation suites to judge real behaviour.

sections.title: The data the AI depends on
sections.body: An assistant is only as good as its data, so I built the engine that creates it.
bullets: Source adapters, normalization, deduplication and quality gates that make missing or contradictory facts visible instead of guessed.
An enrichment pipeline combining rules, model classification and text and image embeddings, taking coverage from 0% to 99.5%.
A multi-million-vector index answering in about 15–21 ms.
Paid model calls are journaled, so an uncertain request is never silently paid for twice.

sections.title: Owning production
bullets: AWS operations (ECS/Fargate, Batch, Step Functions, Lambda, S3, DynamoDB, CloudFormation, IAM) with guarded rollouts, immutable images and cost limits.
The GitHub organisation and CI/CD in GitHub Actions.
iOS releases: code signing, self-hosted Mac build machines, TestFlight and App Store submissions.
Traced a notification pipeline that was failing 100% of the time across the client, backend and provider, and rebuilt it with truthful delivery reporting.

sections.title: Leading the work
sections.body: I review, integrate and release the other engineers' changes, write onboarding and handoff material, and ran a security assessment. I own incidents end to end, including the ones I caused: contain, fix, and write up what changed.

roles.summary: Fintech P&L platform, built solo in 18 days: 5 payment/commerce integrations, ~4,500× faster attribution, 641 orphaned orders recovered.
